Chapter 7: Building a Team of Individuals—Harnessing Diversity of Strengths
So, you’ve started coaching people one-on-one, and now there’s a new challenge—how do you bring all those unique strengths together to create a real team? It’s not about making everyone the same. In fact, the best teams are more like mosaics, where each person adds something different and valuable.
Think of it like a jazz band. Every musician brings their own style, their own skills. The real magic happens when they listen to each other and play in harmony. That’s what great managers do—they help everyone not only understand their own strengths, but also appreciate what their teammates bring to the table. This builds respect and sets the stage for true collaboration.
Let’s talk about some practical ways to build a strengths-based team.
First up, strengths mapping. Imagine putting together a simple chart or visual map that shows each person’s top strengths. It’s a go-to guide whenever you’re assigning tasks or pulling together a project group. Suddenly, it’s clear who’s best at what, and you can play to people’s natural talents instead of asking everyone to fit into the same old mold.
Another approach is role customization. Instead of handing out cookie-cutter roles, tweak responsibilities to match each person’s talents. People end up doing what they do best—and it shows in the results.
Don’t forget the power of peer recognition. Create moments where team members can call out each other’s strengths, especially when someone’s unique ability makes a difference. It’s encouraging, and it helps everyone see the value in being a little different.
And what if the team faces a challenge that doesn’t line up with anyone’s strengths? That’s a chance to come together, talk it out, and figure out how to tackle it as a group. Maybe someone can stretch a little, or maybe you find a creative workaround. Either way, you’re building trust and resilience.
Here’s what happens when you take this approach—performance goes up, trust deepens, and people feel genuinely valued. The team gets more adaptable and differences turn into superpowers, not stumbling blocks.
Of course, it’s not all smooth sailing. Sometimes, strong personalities or very different perspectives can clash. That’s totally normal. The manager’s job is to guide the conversation, keep it healthy, and help everyone find common ground. When handled well, these moments can actually spark new ideas and make the team even stronger.
So, remember—great teams aren’t made up of clones. They’re made up of individuals who know, respect, and harness each other’s strengths. And that’s where the real magic happens.
